> Source: https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/NON_CUSTODIAL.md

# Custody model

Who holds the keys, and who can move the money.

## The test

Two questions decide whether a party is a custodian of someone else's funds:

1. Does it hold the private key?
2. Can it move the balance without the owner's own signature?

For OutLayer the first answer is that wallet keys are derived inside an
enclave and never stored. One exception applies at this stage, set out in
[Governance at this stage](#governance-at-this-stage). The second answer is set by the wallet's policy,
which the owner writes and only the owner can change. This page states
precisely what each party can and cannot do, and how to configure a
wallet so that nothing moves without the owner signing it.

---

## 1. No one holds a private key

A wallet's private key is never generated, stored, or transmitted. It is
derived on demand inside an Intel TDX enclave:

```
master secret (from the NEAR MPC network, never leaves the enclave)
    └── HMAC-SHA256(master, "wallet:{wallet_id}:{chain}")  →  signing key
```

Four properties follow, and each is verifiable without trusting us:

| Property | How it is enforced |
|---|---|
| The master secret is issued by the NEAR MPC network, not by OutLayer | The keystore obtains it through a chain-key derivation call to the MPC contract. The MPC network holds threshold shares; no single node can reconstruct it |
| Attested code obtains it | The keystore submits a TDX attestation quote on chain. The contract verifies the quote's signature chain up to Intel's certification service and checks the build's five measurements against the approved set. Only then does an on-chain DAO vote install the access key the keystore needs. At this stage the DAO account also carries a full-access key: see [Governance at this stage](#governance-at-this-stage) |
| The code does not export a wallet key | The enclave derives and signs. No endpoint, log path, or debug facility emits a wallet's signing key. The one endpoint that returns a private key, callable only by the coordinator, derives separate single-purpose keys under the wallet (a payment check's bearer key, the wallet's trial payment key), because handing those keys over is the product. It cannot derive the wallet's own key. The image is measured, so the code that runs is the code that was approved |
| The infrastructure operator cannot read memory | TDX encrypts enclave memory against the host. An operator can stop a machine; it cannot look inside one |

The consequence for the custody test: there is no key for OutLayer to
hand over, seize, or lose, and no version of our software that behaves
differently without a new on-chain registration that anyone can see.

## 2. Every master secret is issued on chain

Keys and secrets are derived from a master secret, so the question that
matters is how a master comes to exist inside an enclave. It cannot
happen quietly. Each acquisition is a public NEAR transaction:

| Master | Who signs the request | Where it is visible |
|---|---|---|
| Shared root (default wallets) | the keystore's access key on the DAO contract, calling `request_key` | a public transaction. That access key exists only because DAO members voted to install it after the contract verified the enclave's attestation quote |
| Per-customer vault master | the enclave's function-call key on **your own vault contract**, calling `request_master`, which proxies the call to the MPC contract | a public transaction **on your own account** — it appears in your vault's history, not only in ours |

Two things follow. An enclave's authority to obtain a master comes from an
on-chain vote on a verified attestation, so an unapproved build gets
nothing; at this stage the DAO account's full-access key is a second way in
(see [Governance at this stage](#governance-at-this-stage)), and its use is
equally a public transaction. And a customer running a vault does not have to take our word
for how often their root was derived: the transactions are on the
customer's own contract.

Serving is re-checked continuously, not just at issue time. Every signing
operation on a vault-scoped wallet re-reads on-chain state first — the
DAO's verified set, and whether the vault is still under enclave control
— even when the master is already in enclave memory. The moment a
customer finishes recovery, that check fails, the cached master is
evicted, and the keystore refuses to sign. The customer does not have to
ask us to stop.

To be precise about scope: deriving an individual wallet key and
decrypting an individual secret happen inside the enclave from the
master and do not each produce a transaction. What is on chain and
DAO-gated is which builds may hold a master and every event of one being
issued.

## 3. The state that governs your funds lives on chain

The things that decide what may happen to your money are contract state,
not rows in a database we control:

| What | Where it lives | Who can read it | Who can change it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wallet policy | encrypted in the NEAR contract | the enclave decrypts it; our coordinator keeps a readable copy (below) | only its controller account |
| Freeze flag | the same contract entry | anyone | only the controller |
| Secrets | encrypted in the NEAR contract, bound to an owner and a profile | only the enclave decrypts them | their owner |
| Approved builds | the DAO contract | anyone | the DAO owner, at this stage |
| Keystore registrations | the DAO contract | anyone | DAO vote |
| Vault state, exit window, recovery status | your own vault contract | anyone | you, through the parent account |

What our database holds is operational: the job queue, usage counters,
webhook records, the hash of an API key, and a readable copy of each wallet
policy. The coordinator uses that copy to show the policy to its owner and
agent, and for three narrow facts: the hashes of keys authorised for the
wallet, refund addresses for cross-chain deposits, and the approvers for
votes. No signing decision reads it. An attacker who owned that database
entirely could disrupt service and read the policies. They could not
weaken a policy, lift a spending limit, or produce a signature, because
none of those are decided there.

The enclave connects the two halves: it reads the encrypted policy
directly from the chain, decrypts it in memory the host cannot observe,
evaluates it, and only then signs. The rules are enforced by code you can
identify, over data you can read. Two things sit in between: the NEAR RPC
endpoint the enclave reads through, and, for agent custody, our coordinator,
which authenticates the agent and says which wallet a request is for.

## 4. Nothing is signed outside the policy

Every signable action is expressed as a canonical operation, hashed, and
checked against the wallet's policy **inside the enclave** before a
signature exists.

The policy lives encrypted in a NEAR smart contract, and only its
controller can change it, so the rules cannot be edited by our operations
team or anyone who compromises our servers. They can be read: the
coordinator keeps a readable copy (see section 3).

Two facts about the policy matter more than any other on this page:

- **The account that first stores a policy becomes its controller.** Only
  that account can update it, delete it, freeze the wallet, or unfreeze
  it. The signature we produce for a policy write is bound to the exact
  account that will send the transaction, so the controller cannot be set
  to someone else by mistake or by us.
- **A wallet with no policy is unrestricted.** Registration does not
  create rules. Until a policy is stored, whoever holds the API key can
  move the balance within the limits of the primitives enabled by
  default. Storing a policy is the act that creates the constraint.

The controller can also freeze the wallet by sending one transaction
directly to the contract. That path does not involve our API at all, so a
freeze works even if OutLayer is unreachable or uncooperative, except while
the contract is paused (section 11).

## 5. Making the owner's signature mandatory

A policy can name approvers and a threshold. When it does, every
fund-moving operation stops and waits:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "rules": { "limits": { "per_transaction": { "*": "..." } } },
  "approval": {
    "threshold": { "required": 1 },
    "approvers": [
      { "id": "customer.near", "role": "admin", "pubkey": "ed25519:<base58>" }
    ]
  }
}
```

With this policy in place:

- An API key can **propose** a transfer. The response is a pending
  approval, not a transaction.
- The approver signs `approve:{approval_id}:{wallet_pubkey}:{request_hash}`
  as a NEP-413 message with their own wallet.
- The enclave re-derives `request_hash` from the stored canonical
  operation and verifies the signature itself. Our coordinator transports
  the approver's signature; it cannot forge one, and it cannot re-bind it
  to a different operation. What the approval then covers depends on who
  builds the signed message: see the intents operations under
  [Limits we state plainly](#11-limits-we-state-plainly).
- Only then does a signature over the transaction come into existence.

So the owner's signature is not a courtesy step in a user interface. It
is a precondition enforced by measured code, using the public key pinned
in the on-chain policy. An approver entry without a `pubkey` accepts any
full-access key of that account, which the enclave checks on chain.

## 6. The four configurations

| Configuration | Who holds the API credential | Who can move funds | What OutLayer can do alone |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Default, no policy** | whoever registered the wallet | that credential holder, unrestricted | nothing outside the primitives, but the rules are empty — do not run value on this |
| **Policy, no approvers** | the operator of the agent | the credential holder, within the owner's limits, whitelists and caps | nothing outside the policy; the controller can freeze on chain at any time |
| **Policy with the owner as approver** | may be the platform or the agent | **no one without the owner's NEP-413 signature** | nothing; a proposal without the owner's signature never becomes a transaction |
| **Bound personal account** | the agent holds only a scoped extension | the account holder, always | nothing; the account's own keys stay with its holder, and the extension is revoked in one transaction |

These describe who may authorise a transaction. The last column holds for
operations the enclave builds itself; the five intents operations in
section 11 rely on the coordinator for the message they sign, and the
governance keys in section 11 sit outside this table. The next section is
about where the root itself lives, which is a separate choice.

> Availability: the first three configurations are live on mainnet.
> Personal account binding and per-customer vaults are on testnet and
> ship to mainnet with the next release.

## 7. Per-customer vaults: your own custody root

By default a wallet's keys descend from a shared root held by
DAO-approved enclaves. Convenient, and sufficient when the policy already
prevents unilateral movement. It has one property worth naming: the path
back to those keys runs through OutLayer's DAO.

A vault removes that. You deploy a small contract on an account you
create, and that contract becomes the issuer of your master secret:

| Property | What enforces it |
|---|---|
| The vault has no full-access key from the moment it is deployed | It is created in a single atomic transaction; its only key is a function-call key restricted to the MPC derivation call. That key cannot add keys, deploy code, or call anything else |
| The code is a version the DAO approved | The contract is referenced by hash as a published global contract. `outlayer vault verify <vault_id>` runs five independent on-chain checks, including that the hash is on the DAO's whitelist and that no unexpected access key exists |
| Your master is derived through the MPC network from **your** account | The derivation is a transaction on your vault, so its identity, and every issuance of it, are yours to audit |
| You can take it over unilaterally | Your parent account starts recovery; after an exit window you chose at deployment and that is readable on chain before anyone deposits, `finalize_recovery` deletes every OutLayer key and installs your key as the vault's only full-access key |
| You can take it over if we stop | If the DAO declares cessation, the same recovery opens on a fixed delay without any further action from us |

The trade-off is stated plainly on the vaults documentation: after the
exit window, the vault's parent can move the funds. That is the escape
hatch working as designed, and it is why the window is on chain for
counterparties to read before they deposit.

## 8. Leaving OutLayer

A sovereignty claim is only worth what the exit procedure is worth, so
ours is published as an operational runbook rather than a promise:
[`LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md).

After running it you sign for the same wallet addresses with a key you
re-derive locally, and you decrypt the secrets bound to the vault
locally. Nothing changes address, and no value has to be moved to a new
wallet first. What you give up is everything that is OutLayer: minting
new wallets, issuing API keys, our execution layer.

It requires no cooperation from us — not our API, not our dashboard, not
our consent. The contract checks that the caller is the parent account
and that the time window has elapsed, and those are the only conditions.
We cannot cancel a recovery in progress. The runbook also lists what to
store offline beforehand, because a few identifiers (the vault id, the
wallet ids, the MPC verification key) are returned once and are needed to
re-derive specific keys later.

## 9. If you are a platform building on OutLayer

A platform that holds one credential covering every customer wallet is a
custodian of those wallets, whatever the infrastructure underneath is
capable of. The infrastructure does not make that determination; the
configuration does. Three patterns avoid it:

**Customer holds the credential.** Derive the wallet through us and hand
the credential to the customer at creation. The customer calls our API
directly, so your platform is never in the signing path and stores
nothing that can move funds. Best when the customer operates the agent
themselves.

**Platform proposes, customer signs.** The platform keeps a credential
for orchestration and the customer is the approver with a threshold of
one. The platform can assemble and submit work; it cannot complete a
transfer. Best when the platform drives the workflow but must not have
independent control.

**Customer's own account, scoped extension.** The customer's existing
NEAR account keeps its own keys and grants a revocable, policy-bounded
extension to the agent's executor. Best when the customer already holds a
wallet and wants to keep signing with it.

For escrow, hold the funds in an on-chain contract rather than in a
platform wallet. Funds locked by contract rules are not held by anyone,
and the release condition is public. If the release decision needs
judgement rather than a rule, the deciding code can itself run as an
attested OutLayer application: its build is measured, its key exists only
inside the enclave, and every decision carries a TEE attestation. The
decision is then made by code both parties can inspect, not by an
employee of the platform.

**On delegation.** An agent that transacts while its owner is asleep
needs delegated authority by definition. The useful question is not
whether delegation exists but how tightly it is bounded and who can
revoke it. A policy sets per-transaction and cumulative caps, restricts
recipients to a whitelist, limits which primitives are available at all,
and can require the owner's signature above a threshold while allowing
small routine actions to proceed. The owner can tighten or freeze it on
chain without asking anyone. That is a materially different arrangement
from one credential with unrestricted authority over every wallet, and it
is the arrangement we recommend designing toward.

## 10. What you can verify yourself

Nothing on this page asks for trust in a statement by OutLayer:

| Claim | How to check it |
|---|---|
| The wallet's policy is what you wrote | Read the entry in the contract; the ciphertext is public and only the enclave holds the decryption key |
| You are the controller | The controller account is stored with the entry and is what the contract checks on every update, freeze, and delete |
| The keystore is an approved build | Registrations, measurements, and the DAO's votes are on-chain records |
| Your master was issued only when you expect | Every issuance is a transaction; for a vault, it is a transaction on your own contract |
| A specific execution ran in a real enclave | Each call has an attestation containing the TDX quote, verifiable against Intel's certification service |
| The vault is intact and locked | `outlayer vault verify <vault_id>` runs five independent on-chain checks |


### Verifying the code itself

The chain records which build is approved. These steps tie that record
back to source you can read:

| Step | What it proves |
|---|---|
| Release published on GitHub with Sigstore certification | the binary was built by CI from the exact source at that tag; a substituted binary fails the signature |
| Rebuild from that tag | you can compare hashes yourself rather than trusting the published artifact |
| Five TDX measurements (MRTD, RTMR0-3) | firmware, kernel, application and runtime of the enclave that ran, not just the application layer — a debug image with a shell enabled fails even when the application matches |
| The on-chain approved list | the measurements of the enclave that signed for you are on a public, DAO-gated allowlist |
| Per-execution attestation | the TDX quote for that specific call, signed up to Intel's certification chain |
| `outlayer-verify` | an open-source binary that re-runs these checks on your own machine. Intel's root certificate is compiled into it, so a chain that does not end at Intel fails regardless of what we serve. It needs no account, no API key and no key material |

The full walkthrough, including both deployment methods and the
registration flow, is at https://app.outlayer.ai/docs/trust-verification.

## 11. Limits we state plainly

- **A wallet with no policy is unrestricted.** This is the single most
  important sentence on this page. Store a policy before funding a wallet.
- **Five intents operations carry a residual trust in our coordinator.**
  For transfers, contract calls, withdrawals to a NEAR account and intents
  transfers, the enclave builds the signed message from the approved
  operation, so what is signed is exactly what was approved. For swaps,
  cross-chain withdrawals, confidential-intents operations (shield,
  unshield, transfer, withdraw, swap), limit orders and payment checks, the
  coordinator supplies the intents message: the route and deposit address
  come from a third-party solver at execution time, and a payment check's
  receiving account is named by the coordinator. The
  enclave checks the policy, per-transaction caps and approvals against the
  token and amount the operation declares, pins the message to an intents
  verifier (`intents.near` or `intents.far`), and signs the message as
  supplied, without parsing it. A compromised coordinator could therefore
  have the enclave sign a different intent for a wallet on which these
  operations are enabled. All five are denied by default once a policy is
  stored; a wallet with no policy allows them.
- **Cumulative limits are best-effort under concurrency.** Daily, hourly
  and monthly caps are counted outside the enclave, so a burst of
  simultaneous requests can overshoot one. Per-transaction limits,
  multisig and freeze are enforced inside the enclave and are exact.
- **A contract pause blocks freezing.** The contract owner can pause the
  contract; while it is paused, writes to it fail, `freeze_wallet`
  included. The enclave does not read the pause, so signing continues.
- **We can refuse service.** An operator can stop executing or shut down
  infrastructure. Outside the governance keys below it cannot move funds,
  and with a vault it cannot prevent you from taking over your own keys.

### Governance at this stage

While volumes are small, governance runs on single keys held by OutLayer.
Every use of them is a public NEAR transaction.

- **The DAO account carries a full-access key.** `dao.outlayer.near` holds
  one full-access key besides the keystore keys installed by vote. A
  transaction signed with it passes the `request_key` check, so its holder
  can obtain the shared master secret outside any enclave.
- **One account approves builds.** Enclave measurements are approved by
  the DAO owner alone, and the DAO has one member.
- **Contracts upgrade by key.** The policy contract (`outlayer.near`), the
  DAO contract and the worker registration contract are each redeployed
  with a full-access key, without a vote or a delay. A redeploy of the
  policy contract can rewrite or remove any stored policy.

Before significant funds go through, these move to the DAO: the
full-access keys are removed, measurement approval, membership changes and
contract upgrades go to a vote, and the DAO takes independent members.

---

<!-- source: VAULTS.md -->
> Source: https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/VAULTS.md

# Sovereign Vaults — Architecture & Recovery Procedure

OutLayer's per-customer master keys with on-chain recoverability.
This document describes the **architecture**, the **trust model**,
and the two **recovery procedures**. The customer-facing how-to is
https://app.outlayer.ai/docs/vaults and `outlayer vault --help`; the
step-by-step exit runbook is [`docs/LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md).

## Why vaults exist

By default, every wallet key and encrypted secret on OutLayer is
derived from a shared **OutLayer default master**, held inside the
keystore-worker's TEE. Zero customer setup, shared infrastructure. The
only path back to those keys is an enclave that OutLayer's keystore
DAO approves.

A **vault** replaces that shared master with a per-customer master
derived through NEAR's MPC network from the customer's own account,
with two on-chain exits back to the customer:

1. **Cessation recovery** — the keystore DAO declares
   `is_ceased() == true`; anyone can start the recovery; fixed 7-day
   delay; the parent account finalizes.
2. **Unilateral recovery** — the customer's parent NEAR account
   exits at any time without DAO involvement, after an exit window
   chosen at deploy (1–30 days in the production build).

Finalizing either recovery atomically deletes every OutLayer key on
the vault and installs a key the parent supplies as the vault's only
full-access key.

## Components

| Layer | Responsibility | Path |
|---|---|---|
| **Vault contract** | Per-customer NEAR sub-account holding the TEE function-call key, the `request_master` MPC proxy and the recovery state machine | `vault-contract/` |
| **Keystore-DAO** | Whitelists vault WASM hashes, tracks `verified_vaults`, `banned_vaults`, `ceased_operations` | `keystore-dao-contract/src/lib.rs` |
| **Keystore-worker** | Per-vault master cache with lazy MPC CKD load and a per-request serving gate; `/derive-vault-tee-key`, `/sign-vault-verification`, `/admin/ban-vault`, `/admin/evict-customer`, `/admin/loaded-vaults` | `keystore-worker/src/mpc_ckd.rs`, `vault_verifier.rs`, `api_support.rs` (router in `api.rs`) |
| **Vault-checker WASI** | Open-source, independent implementation of the vault checks | `wasi-examples/vault-checker/` |
| **Coordinator** | `/customer/derive-tee-key`, `/customer/sign-verification`, `/customer/register`, `/register {vault_id}`, `/internal/vault-event`, and the `/call` vault-serving pre-check | `outlayer-coordinator` (private repo): `src/wallet/handlers.rs`, `src/handlers/call.rs` |
| **CLI** | `outlayer vault {init,resume,status,verify,initiate-recovery,initiate-unilateral-recovery,finalize-recovery,set-exit-window,unlocked-add-key}` | [outlayer-cli](https://github.com/out-layer/cli) `src/commands/vault.rs` |
| **Dashboard** | `/vault` management page; vault scope on the secrets and wallet pages | [dashboard](https://github.com/out-layer/dashboard) `app/vault/page.tsx`, `lib/vault.ts` |
| **Monitor** | Reads chain events: forwards vault log events to the coordinator, evicts cached masters on finalize, bans a vault on duplicate MPC calls | `outlayer-monitor/` |
| **Recovery tool** | Customer-side MPC CKD, wallet-key re-derivation, local secret decryption | `scripts/customer-recovery/` |

## Atomic deploy flow

The parent account signs a single transaction with five actions that
either all succeed or all roll back:

```
receiver = vault.<customer.near>
actions  = [
    CreateAccount,
    Transfer(1 NEAR),                       // storage (~0.004 NEAR) + standing gas reserve for MPC calls
    UseGlobalContract(approved_code_hash),  // NEP-591: the WASM lives in the global registry
    FunctionCall("new", {parent, keystore_dao, mpc_contract,
                         initial_tee_pubkey, initial_exit_window}),
    AddKey(tee_pubkey,
           FunctionCall { receiver: vault.<customer.near>,
                          methods: ["request_master"],
                          allowance: unlimited }),
]
```

`new()` requires the vault to be a direct sub-account of `parent`, so
a vault cannot name an unrelated account as its parent. The code hash
is the newest non-deprecated entry of
`keystore_dao.list_approved_vault_versions()`.

A half-deployed vault (account exists, contract not initialised, or
TEE key absent) cannot exist: every failure mode collapses into
"sub-account never existed; retry safely".

The CLI calls two coordinator endpoints around the deploy:

1. `POST /customer/derive-tee-key {vault_id}` — BEFORE the deploy, so
   the `AddKey` action installs the right TEE pubkey (deterministic,
   computed inside the TEE; see Layer 1 below).
2. `POST /customer/sign-verification {vault_id}` — AFTER the deploy.
   The keystore re-runs its vault checks (`vault_verifier.rs`: not
   banned, code hash approved, exactly one access key and it is the
   `request_master` function-call key, `unlocked == false`, no
   recovery in flight, expected `keystore_dao`) and submits
   `mark_vault_verified` on the DAO contract.

`outlayer vault resume <vault>` re-runs step 2 idempotently. Custody
wallets are minted separately, any number per vault, with
`POST /register {"vault_id": "<vault>"}` (returns `wallet_id`,
`api_key`, `near_account_id`) or `POST /customer/register
{"vault_account_id": "<vault>", "webhook_url": "..."}`; both require
`is_vault_verified == true`.

## Two-layer key derivation

```
Layer 1 (TEE function-call key, derived from the OutLayer default master):
    tee_keypair = ed25519(HMAC-SHA256(default_master, "outlayer.near:{vault_id}"))
    installed on the vault as a function-call key on (vault, ["request_master"])

Layer 2 (per-vault master, MPC CKD called FROM the vault):
    derivation_path = hex(HMAC-SHA256(default_master, "secret-path:vault-master:{vault_id}"))
    tx: signer = vault_id (Layer 1 key) → vault.request_master({request})
        → mpc_contract.request_app_private_key({derivation_path,
                                                app_public_key = ephemeral BLS12-381 G1,
                                                domain_id = 2}), 1 yoctoNEAR from the vault
    app_id = SHA3-256("near-mpc v0.1.0 app_id derivation:" + vault_id + "," + derivation_path)
    master = HKDF-SHA256(decrypted 48-byte G1 secret) → 32 bytes
```

`request_master` accepts only `predecessor == current_account_id`
(a transaction signed by a key on the vault itself), and refuses once
the vault is unlocked. The proxy exists because MPC requires 1
yoctoNEAR and a function-call key cannot attach a deposit.

Determinism: same vault id + same default master → same
derivation path → same MPC-derived master, whichever approved keystore
runs the derivation. MPC binds the result to the predecessor (the
vault account), so the same path from another account yields an
unrelated secret.

The derivation path is unguessable before the keystore's first CKD
call and is public in that call's arguments afterwards. Knowing it
gives nothing without the ability to sign a transaction as the vault.

Wallet keys and secret-encryption keys under a vault use the same
recipes as the default master, with the per-vault master as the HMAC
key: `wallet:{wallet_id}:near` (ed25519), `wallet:{wallet_id}:evm`
(secp256k1, one key for every EVM chain), `wallet:{wallet_id}:solana`
(ed25519); secrets use ECIES with the recipient key derived from
`"ecies:" + seed`.

## Serving gate

On every operation that names a vault, the keystore reads the chain
before it serves (`mpc_ckd.rs::ensure_customer_loaded` →
`assert_serving_allowed`):

- `keystore_dao.is_vault_verified(vault)` — false for unverified and
  banned vaults;
- `vault.get_state().unlocked == false`.

Either failing evicts the cached master and refuses. The CKD call is
made only after both pass, so the master is first derived after
`mark_vault_verified`. The coordinator runs the same two checks on
`/call` for Project-bound secrets that carry a vault binding and
answers `423 Locked` for an unlocked vault, `403` for an unverified
one.

## Trust model

### What the vault guarantees

- After the atomic deploy the vault holds **only** the TEE
  function-call key, restricted to `vault.request_master`. That key
  cannot add keys, deploy code, transfer funds, or call any other
  method. The parent holds **no key on the vault account**.
- The approved contract has no method that deploys code, and adds
  keys only in `callback_add_tee_key` (DAO-approved keystore keys,
  function-call on `request_master` only, max 32) and in the
  recovery swap / `unlocked_add_key` (parent, after unlock). Audit
  checklist: `vault-contract/src/lib.rs` module doc.
- Every derivation of the per-vault master is a transaction on the
  customer's own vault account, visible in its history.
- The only paths from "deployed, verified" to "parent-controlled" are
  the two recoveries below. Both impose a delay (exit window ≥ 1 day;
  cessation 7 days) and are visible on chain in `get_state().recovery`,
  which `outlayer vault status` prints.

### What it does not guarantee at this stage

The Layer 1 key and the derivation path are derived from the OutLayer
default master. A keystore build the DAO approves can therefore derive
any locked vault's TEE key and obtain its per-vault master through
`request_master`. Today approving keystore measurements is owner-only,
the DAO has one member and its account also has a full-access key
(see [NON_CUSTODIAL.md — Governance at this stage](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/NON_CUSTODIAL.md#governance-at-this-stage)).
So while a vault is locked, the customer still trusts OutLayer's
governance not to approve a build that misuses a master. What the
vault adds is that every such derivation is a public transaction on
the customer's account, and that the customer can leave without
OutLayer's cooperation.

Recovery does not rotate keys: the master the customer recovers is
the master the keystore used, and every wallet keeps its address. A
customer who leaves because they distrust a past keystore build should
move funds to fresh keys after recovering.

### Customer vs end-user

The end-user (the customer's customer) interacts with the customer's
app. OutLayer is the customer's TEE infrastructure provider, not a
counterparty to end-users. **Unilateral recovery is a customer escape
hatch, not an end-user protection.** A customer can regain full
control of the vault:

1. Call `unilateral_initiate_recovery`, wait
   `unilateral_exit_window_secs` (set at deploy, on chain).
2. Call `finalize_recovery(new_pubkey)` — the vault now has the
   customer's full-access key and no OutLayer key.
3. Sign `mpc_contract.request_app_private_key` from the vault with the
   public derivation path and receive the per-vault master — and with
   it every wallet key and every secret encrypted under that vault.

That is the sovereignty feature working as designed. For end-users:

- Treat the customer as you would if they ran custody themselves:
  after the exit window they CAN move the funds.
- Read `unilateral_exit_window_secs` via `outlayer vault status
  <vault_id>` BEFORE depositing. A long window is a promise not to
  exit for that long; the 1-day minimum reserves a quick exit.
- `get_recovery_state()` is observable in real time; a watcher gets
  the full exit window of warning before the customer gains control.
- A `parent` controlled by a multisig or a contract shifts the trust
  from "the customer" to "the customer's signers".

### Duplicate-derivation monitor

`outlayer-monitor` watches `request_app_private_key` receipts to the
MPC contract. Two receipts with the same `(predecessor vault,
derivation_path)` within 600 blocks (~10 minutes; configurable) trigger
the keystore's `/admin/ban-vault` (which submits
`keystore_dao.ban_vault` and evicts the cached master) and an alert
(Slack, Telegram or stdout). A banned vault fails `is_vault_verified`
and is refused by the serving gate; `unban_vault` is DAO-member-only.

The same monitor forwards vault log events (`recovery_*`,
`exit_window_set_*`, `vault_tee_key_added`, …), each re-checked against
RPC, to the coordinator's `/internal/vault-event`, and on
`recovery_finalized_*` asks the keystore to evict that vault's master.
The serving gate refuses an unlocked vault on its own; eviction only
clears memory sooner.

## Recovery procedures

### Cessation recovery

Used when OutLayer stops operating. Starting it is permissionless and
gated on DAO state; finalizing it is parent-only.

```
DAO member → keystore_dao.declare_cessation()
              [ceased_operations = true; any single DAO member, reversible]

Anyone     → vault.initiate_recovery()
              ↓ cross-contract is_ceased() check
              ↓ if true: recovery = {trigger: Cessation,
                                     finalize_after: now + 7d,
                                     finalize_before: finalize_after + 7d}

(7-day delay)

Parent     → vault.finalize_recovery(new_parent_pubkey)
              ↓ is_ceased() re-checked; if the DAO revoked cessation,
              ↓ the recovery is cleared and the vault stays locked
              ↓ else: atomic batch on the vault account —
              ↓   DeleteKey(initial_tee_key), DeleteKey(each registered TEE key),
              ↓   AddFullAccessKey(new_parent_pubkey)
              ↓ callback_after_swap: unlocked = true, recovery = None
```

After a revocation the recovery can be started again once cessation is
declared again.

### Unilateral recovery

Customer-driven exit. No DAO involvement.

```
Parent     → vault.set_exit_window(secs)             [optional; 1d–30d; future recoveries only]
Parent     → vault.unilateral_initiate_recovery()
              [recovery = {trigger: Unilateral,
                           finalize_after: now + unilateral_exit_window_secs,
                           finalize_before: finalize_after + 7d}]

(exit window)

Parent     → vault.finalize_recovery(new_parent_pubkey)
              [same atomic key swap as above, no DAO check]
```

Common rules (both triggers):

- One recovery at a time.
- The window is frozen at initiate time; `set_exit_window` during a
  recovery only affects later ones.
- Finalizing before `finalize_after` panics with no state change.
- A finalize after `finalize_before` clears the recovery (the vault
  stays locked) and must be started again.
- If the swap batch fails (e.g. `new_parent_pubkey` already on the
  account), state is unchanged and the parent can retry with another
  key inside the window.
- If the parent account is lost, the vault stays locked forever, even
  after cessation. Finalize is parent-only so that no one watching the
  chain can substitute their own key.

`unlocked_add_key` adds further keys after unlock (parent only).

## Governance

The DAO's vault-version registry is quorum-gated:
`approve_vault_version(hash, label, audit_url)` and
`revoke_vault_version(hash)` execute when `approval_threshold` (>50%
of DAO members) distinct members have voted. Votes are keyed on the
hash; the first proposer's `(label, audit_url)` is locked and later
voters must pass the same values. Votes from accounts no longer in the
DAO are dropped before counting. `deprecate_vault_version` is
single-member: deprecation keeps the hash approved (existing vaults
keep working) and only steers new deployments away from it.
`declare_cessation`, `revoke_cessation` and `unban_vault` are
single-member.

With the DAO at one member, every one of these is a single-signer
action today, and the DAO account's full-access key can change the
contract itself.

## Operational considerations

- **Balance:** `outlayer vault init` transfers 1 NEAR to the vault.
  Storage is ~0.004 NEAR (state only; the WASM is a global contract).
  The rest is a standing reserve: each `request_master` call must
  prepay its attached gas from the vault's balance (most of it is
  refunded), and the keystore re-derives the master after every
  keystore restart, because the cache lives in enclave memory. A vault
  that cannot cover the prepayment cannot derive its master; top it up.
- **TEE key cap:** `MAX_REGISTERED_TEE_KEYS = 32`. `propose_tee_key` is
  permissionless but accepts only DAO-approved keystore keys; the
  parent can free slots with `clear_unused_tee_keys`.
- **Webhooks:** `POST /customer/register` takes `webhook_url`. The
  coordinator sends `vault_registered` and `vault_verified` itself;
  on-chain transitions (`recovery_initiated_*`, `recovery_finalized_*`,
  `recovery_window_expired`, `recovery_cancelled_dao_revoked`,
  `exit_window_set`, `vault_banned`, `vault_unbanned`,
  `vault_tee_key_added`) arrive through `outlayer-monitor` →
  `/internal/vault-event`.

## Cross-references

- https://app.outlayer.ai/docs/vaults — customer-facing how-to
- [`docs/LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md) — sovereign exit runbook
- [`docs/NON_CUSTODIAL.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/NON_CUSTODIAL.md) — custody and governance model
- [`vault-contract/README.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/vault-contract/README.md) — contract API, events, build
- [`scripts/customer-recovery/README.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/scripts/customer-recovery/README.md) — recovery tool
- `tests/vault_e2e.sh`, `tests/vault_recovery_e2e.sh` — CLI deploy and contract recovery state machine on testnet
- `tests/unified_vault_e2e.sh` (V1–V6) — isolation, multi-wallet, sovereign exit with offline re-derivation, secret decryption after recovery

<!-- source: docs/LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md -->
> Source: https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/LEAVING_OUTLAYER.md

# Leaving OutLayer (Sovereign Exit)

This document is the **operational runbook** for taking a per-customer
vault out from under OutLayer's keystore and continuing to use the
same wallet addresses and the same on-chain secrets without OutLayer
infrastructure.

It targets two audiences:

1. **Customers** who have deployed a vault with `outlayer vault init`
   and want a procedure to follow if OutLayer becomes unavailable,
   untrustworthy, or simply unwanted.
2. **Operators / auditors** reviewing the sovereignty guarantee —
   each step points to the contract / keystore code that enforces it.

For the architecture and trust model of vaults, see
[`VAULTS.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/VAULTS.md) and https://app.outlayer.ai/docs/vaults.

---

## The promise, and its limits

After you run the procedure in this document:

| Capability | Before (OutLayer in the loop) | After (sovereign exit) |
|---|---|---|
| Sign transactions for your custody wallet(s) | OutLayer keystore signs via `/wallet/v1/*` | You sign locally with a re-derived key |
| Decrypt secrets bound to the vault | OutLayer worker / keystore decrypts in TEE | You decrypt locally with the recovered master |
| Mint new wallets / API keys, run code | Coordinator | Not available — you've left OutLayer |
| Control the vault account and its balance | TEE function-call key only | Your full-access key only |

The unilateral exit needs no cooperation from OutLayer: not its API,
not its dashboard, not its DAO. It needs your parent account, the NEAR
RPC, the NEAR MPC network, and the open-source tools in this repo and
in [outlayer-cli](https://github.com/out-layer/cli).

What the exit does **not** do:

- **It does not rotate any key.** The master you recover is the master
  the keystore used; every wallet keeps its address and its key. The
  exit ends OutLayer's ability to derive the master again, not any
  copy obtained before. While the vault was locked, a keystore build
  approved by OutLayer's DAO could obtain the master (see
  [VAULTS.md — What it does not guarantee at this stage](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/VAULTS.md#what-it-does-not-guarantee-at-this-stage)).
  If you are leaving because you distrust a past keystore, move funds
  to fresh keys after Phase B and re-encrypt your secrets.
- **The wallet policy no longer applies.** Limits, allowlists and
  approvals were enforced by the keystore before it signed. A key you
  hold locally signs anything.

---

## What you need to keep before exit

Do this once when you deploy each vault and store the result offline:

1. **Vault id** — printed by `outlayer vault init`. Example:
   `vault.alice.near`.
2. **Parent NEAR account credentials** — the account in the vault's
   `parent` field. Only it can initiate a unilateral recovery and
   finalize any recovery. Treat it like a cold-storage wallet.
3. **`wallet_id`** (UUID) and **`near_account_id`** of every custody
   wallet minted under the vault. `POST /register {"vault_id": "..."}`
   returns them once; save the response. A wallet's NEAR key is
   `HMAC-SHA256(per_vault_master, "wallet:<wallet_id>:near")`, so
   without the UUID you cannot reach a specific wallet's key. Wallets
   created by a signed claim (`PUT /wallet/v1/api-key` or `Bearer
   near:` with a `vault_id`) have a deterministic id you can recompute
   offline with `customer-recovery compute-wallet-id --account-id
   <acct> --seed <seed> --vault-id <vault>`.
4. **Profile + accessor of every vault-bound secret** — needed to look
   up its ciphertext on chain after exit.
5. **(Optional) `MPC_PUBLIC_KEY`** — the `bls12381g2:...` key the
   recovery tool uses to verify that the master came from the MPC
   network. It is public; read it from the MPC contract (domain 2):

   ```bash
   near contract call-function as-read-only v1.signer public_key \
     json-args '{"domain_id": 2}' network-config mainnet now
   # testnet: v1.signer-prod.testnet ... network-config testnet
   ```

   Store the answer so the recovery needs no lookup later.

Everything above except the parent's private key is public
information.

---

## The procedure in short

```bash
# 0. Build the tool (once).
cd scripts/customer-recovery && cargo build --release && cd -
BIN=./scripts/customer-recovery/target/release/customer-recovery

# 1. Start the on-chain exit (parent signs; `outlayer login mainnet` as the parent first).
outlayer vault initiate-unilateral-recovery vault.alice.near

# 2. Wait until `finalize_after` (shown in ns by `outlayer vault status vault.alice.near`).

# 3. Generate the key that will own the vault, then hand the vault to it.
mkdir -m 700 -p ~/.outlayer-recovery
"$BIN" generate-key > ~/.outlayer-recovery/vault.alice.near.json
outlayer vault finalize-recovery vault.alice.near \
  "$(jq -r .public_key ~/.outlayer-recovery/vault.alice.near.json)"

# 4. Recover the per-vault master.
VAULT_PRIVATE_KEY=$(jq -r .private_key ~/.outlayer-recovery/vault.alice.near.json) \
MPC_PUBLIC_KEY='bls12381g2:...' \
  "$BIN" --vault-id vault.alice.near --from-chain \
    --rpc-url https://rpc.mainnet.fastnear.com \
    --mpc-contract v1.signer \
    --nearblocks-url https://api.nearblocks.io
# stdout ends with: master_hex=<64 hex chars>
```

The rest (re-deriving wallets, decrypting secrets) is local.

[`scripts/customer-recovery/walkthrough.sh`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/scripts/customer-recovery/walkthrough.sh)
runs steps 0–4 for a vault that is **not yet unlocked**: it checks
that the logged-in account is the parent, skips initiate if a recovery
is already running, sleeps until `finalize_after`, finalizes and
confirms `unlocked == true`. Run it as
`VAULT_ID=vault.alice.near NETWORK=mainnet MPC_PUBLIC_KEY=... ./walkthrough.sh`.
It always generates a new key file and refuses to overwrite an
existing one, so once a finalize has landed, run step 4 directly with
the key you finalized with.

---

## Step-by-step

### Phase A — On-chain exit (parent-signed)

#### A.1 Confirm the vault is yours and locked

```bash
outlayer vault status vault.alice.near
```

Required fields:
- `Parent: <your_account>` — must be the account whose key you hold.
  `unilateral_initiate_recovery` and `finalize_recovery` both require
  `env::predecessor_account_id() == self.parent`.
- `Status: locked (TEE-controlled)` — if it already says
  `UNLOCKED (recovered)`, skip to Phase B.
- `Recovery: none in progress` — if a recovery is running, see
  "What if someone front-ran me?" below.

If `Parent` is wrong, **stop**: every following call will be rejected.

#### A.2 Initiate unilateral recovery

```bash
outlayer vault initiate-unilateral-recovery vault.alice.near
```

The contract records `finalize_after = now + exit_window` and
`finalize_before = finalize_after + 7 days`. The exit window was set
at deploy (`--exit-window`, default `24h`; the production contract
accepts 1 day to 30 days). `outlayer vault set-exit-window` (parent
only, same range) changes it for FUTURE recoveries; a recovery in
flight keeps the timestamps it was initiated with.

#### A.3 Wait the exit window

Real time. Finalizing before `finalize_after` panics with `recovery
delay not yet elapsed` and changes nothing. You then have 7 days to
finalize; a finalize after `finalize_before` clears the recovery (the
vault stays locked) and you start again at A.2.

#### A.4 Generate the key that will own the vault

```bash
mkdir -m 700 -p ~/.outlayer-recovery
./scripts/customer-recovery/target/release/customer-recovery generate-key \
    > ~/.outlayer-recovery/vault.alice.near.json
chmod 600 ~/.outlayer-recovery/vault.alice.near.json
```

The output is `{public_key, private_key}` JSON in the format
`near-cli-rs` uses. This keypair becomes the **only** full-access key
on the vault. Back the file up offline immediately: losing it after
finalize means losing the vault.

#### A.5 Finalize — atomic key swap

```bash
NEW_PUBKEY=$(jq -r .public_key ~/.outlayer-recovery/vault.alice.near.json)
outlayer vault finalize-recovery vault.alice.near "$NEW_PUBKEY"
```

What happens on chain (`vault-contract/src/lib.rs`):

1. Parent-only check (`predecessor == self.parent`).
2. Window check (`finalize_after <= now <= finalize_before`).
3. One Promise batch on the vault account (`dispatch_swap`):
   `DeleteKey(initial_tee_key)`, `DeleteKey(k)` for every entry in
   `registered_tee_keys`, `AddFullAccessKey(new_pubkey)`.
4. `callback_after_swap` sets `unlocked = true` and clears `recovery`
   only if the batch succeeded. If it failed (e.g. the pubkey is
   already a key on the account), state is unchanged and you can
   retry with a fresh keypair inside the same window.

After this transaction OutLayer has **no access key on the vault
account**, and `request_master` refuses an unlocked vault, so the
per-vault master cannot be derived again by anyone but you. The
keystore checks `unlocked` on every operation that names the vault,
refuses, and evicts the master from memory. The coordinator answers
`/call/<owner>/<project>` requests whose Project secret is bound to
this vault with **HTTP 423 Locked** before dispatching any work.

#### A.6 Confirm the unlock landed

```bash
outlayer vault status vault.alice.near
# Status:          UNLOCKED (recovered)
# Recovery:        none in progress
```

`vault.get_state().unlocked == true` is the on-chain ground truth.

---

### Phase B — Local key derivation

From here you only need a NEAR RPC, the MPC contract and (for
auto-discovery) a NEARblocks-compatible indexer.

#### B.1 Recover the per-vault master via MPC CKD

```bash
export VAULT_PRIVATE_KEY=$(jq -r .private_key ~/.outlayer-recovery/vault.alice.near.json)
export MPC_PUBLIC_KEY='bls12381g2:...'   # from step 5 of "What you need to keep"

./scripts/customer-recovery/target/release/customer-recovery \
    --vault-id vault.alice.near \
    --from-chain \
    --rpc-url https://rpc.mainnet.fastnear.com \
    --mpc-contract v1.signer \
    --nearblocks-url https://api.nearblocks.io
unset VAULT_PRIVATE_KEY
```

The tool's defaults are testnet (`v1.signer-prod.testnet`,
`rpc.testnet.fastnear.com`, `api-testnet.nearblocks.io`); pass the
mainnet values as above. `--mpc-domain-id` defaults to `2`.

What `--from-chain` does: reads the vault's 20 most recent
transactions from NEARblocks, takes the newest one signed by the vault
that calls `request_master` (or `request_app_private_key`), and reads
`request.derivation_path` from its arguments. The path is
`hex(HMAC-SHA256(default_master, "secret-path:vault-master:<vault_id>"))`
— unguessable before the keystore's first derivation, public in that
transaction afterwards. If auto-discovery finds nothing (more than 20
newer transactions, or the indexer is unavailable), pass
`--derivation-path` yourself; see
[`scripts/customer-recovery/README.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/scripts/customer-recovery/README.md#auto-discovery-of-derivation_path).

The tool then signs `request_app_private_key` to the MPC contract
**from the vault** with your new key (150 TGas, 1 yoctoNEAR; the vault
must hold enough NEAR to prepay the gas), decrypts the response with a
fresh ephemeral BLS12-381 key, verifies it with a pairing check against
`MPC_PUBLIC_KEY`, and HKDF-stretches the 48-byte secret to the 32-byte
master. MPC binds the result to `(vault account, derivation_path)`, so
this is the same master the keystore obtained through `request_master`.

Output ends with:

```
master_hex=<64 hex chars>
```

**Save the master.** Anyone who has it can derive every wallet key and
decrypt every secret of the vault.

If the keystore never derived a master for this vault (no wallet or
secret was ever served), there is no past transaction and nothing
encrypted under it.

#### B.2 Re-derive each wallet's keys

For every NEAR wallet you minted under the vault:

```bash
./scripts/customer-recovery/target/release/customer-recovery derive-wallet-key \
    --master "$MASTER_HEX" \
    --wallet-id "<the UUID you saved at registration>"
```

Output is JSON:

```json
{
  "wallet_id": "...",
  "near_address": "<hex>",
  "public_key": "ed25519:...",
  "private_key": "ed25519:..."
}
```

`near_address` MUST equal the `near_account_id` the coordinator
returned at registration. If it differs, the derivation recipe and the
keystore have diverged — file a bug.

You can now sign any NEAR transaction as that wallet:

```bash
near tokens "<near_address>" send-near alice.near '0.01 NEAR' \
    network-config mainnet \
    sign-with-plaintext-private-key 'ed25519:...' send
```

Balances held for the wallet in other contracts (for example
`intents.near`) belong to the same account and move with transactions
signed by this key.

`derive-wallet-key` covers the NEAR key only. The wallet's other chain
keys use the same master with these seeds (keystore
`api.rs::wallet_seed`, `crypto.rs`); the tool has no subcommand for
them, so derive them with any HMAC-SHA256 implementation:

| Chain | Seed | Key |
|---|---|---|
| NEAR | `wallet:<wallet_id>:near` | ed25519 seed = HMAC output |
| EVM (all EVM chains, one address) | `wallet:<wallet_id>:evm` | secp256k1 secret scalar = HMAC output (big-endian) |
| Solana | `wallet:<wallet_id>:solana` | ed25519 seed = HMAC output |

#### B.3 Decrypt each on-chain secret

For every vault-bound secret (stored with `outlayer secrets set
--vault-id <vault>` or from the dashboard with vault scope):

```bash
# 1. Fetch the ciphertext from the contract.
ARGS=$(jq -cn --arg pid 'alice.near/my-project' --arg owner 'alice.near' --arg profile 'prod' \
    '{accessor: {Project: {project_id: $pid}}, profile: $profile, owner: $owner}')
ARGS_B64=$(printf '%s' "$ARGS" | base64 | tr -d '\n')
CIPHERTEXT=$(curl -s https://rpc.mainnet.fastnear.com -X POST \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":1,\"method\":\"query\",\"params\":{\"request_type\":\"call_function\",\"finality\":\"final\",\"account_id\":\"outlayer.near\",\"method_name\":\"get_secrets\",\"args_base64\":\"$ARGS_B64\"}}" \
    | jq -r '.result.result | implode' \
    | jq -r '.encrypted_secrets')

# 2. Decrypt with the recovered master and the accessor's seed.
./scripts/customer-recovery/target/release/customer-recovery decrypt-secret \
    --master "$MASTER_HEX" \
    --seed 'project:alice.near/my-project:alice.near' \
    --ciphertext-base64 "$CIPHERTEXT"
```

Output is the plaintext JSON object you stored (`{"KEY":"value", ...}`).
`get_secret_vault(accessor, profile, owner)` on the same contract
returns the vault a secret is bound to.

The seed is fixed per accessor (keystore `api.rs`):
- **Project** (`--project owner/name`): `project:<owner>/<name>:<owner>`
- **Repo**: `<normalized_repo>:<owner>:<branch>`, or
  `<normalized_repo>:<owner>` when the secret has no branch
- **WasmHash** (`--wasm-hash <sha256>`): `wasm_hash:<hash>:<owner>`

`decrypt-secret` detects the format: ECIES v1 (first byte `0x01`; what
the CLI and the dashboard write), otherwise the older symmetric
ChaCha20-Poly1305 format, which the keystore also still reads.

---

## What survives the exit

| Artifact | You have | OutLayer has |
|---|---|---|
| Vault account and its balance | the only full-access key | no key |
| Per-vault master (32 bytes) | recovered locally | no way to derive it again; an honest keystore has evicted it from memory |
| Wallet private keys | derivable from master + wallet_id | derivable only from the master |
| On-chain ciphertext of secrets | readable + decryptable | readable; decryptable only with the master |
| `parent` field on the vault | unchanged (your account) | — |

A copy of the master taken before the exit is not affected by it — see
"What the exit does not do" above.

---

## What you give up

- **OutLayer's keystore signing API** — `/wallet/v1/*` requests for
  wallets under this vault are refused: the keystore reports the vault
  as unlocked. You sign locally instead.
- **`/call/<owner>/<project>` with vault-bound secrets** — refused with
  HTTP 423. Execution that does not use vault-bound secrets is
  unaffected.
- **The dashboard** shows the vault as `UNLOCKED (recovered)`. Unlock
  is one-way: no method re-locks a vault.

You can deploy a **new** vault under the same parent at any time, on
another sub-account name (`outlayer vault init --name <other>`).

---

## What if someone front-ran me?

They can't take the vault.

`finalize_recovery` panics with `only the parent account can finalize
recovery` for any other caller, before reading or changing state. A
watcher who sees your `finalize_after` pass cannot substitute their
own key; you can finalize at any point until `finalize_before`.

`unilateral_initiate_recovery` is parent-only as well.

`initiate_recovery` (the cessation path) is permissionless, but
`callback_initiate` refuses unless the DAO has declared cessation. A
recovery someone else started while cessation is declared still ends
with **your** key, because only the parent can finalize it. A
cessation recovery that is in flight blocks a unilateral one (one
recovery at a time) until it is finalized or expires.

---

## Trade-off the design makes

If your **parent account becomes unavailable** (lost key, deceased
operator, lost multisig signers), the vault stays locked forever, even
after DAO cessation. The alternative — anyone can finalize — would let
a third party install their own key at finalize time.

For high-value deployments, give the parent account its own recovery
(multisig, social recovery) out-of-band.

---

## Verification check-list (for auditors)

The exit rests on five properties, each testable on its own:

1. **Parent-only `finalize_recovery`** — `require!(predecessor ==
   self.parent)` before any state change. Tests:
   `vault-contract/src/lib.rs` unit tests
   `finalize_recovery_rejects_non_parent_unilateral` /
   `_cessation`; sandbox test
   `vault-contract/tests/integration.rs::unilateral_finalize_rejects_non_parent_after_window`.
2. **Atomic key swap** — `dispatch_swap` issues `DeleteKey(*) +
   AddFullAccessKey(new_pubkey)` in one batch; state changes only in
   `callback_after_swap` on success. Tests:
   `callback_after_swap_commits_state_on_success`,
   `callback_after_swap_leaves_state_untouched_on_failure`.
3. **Keystore refuses unlocked vaults** —
   `keystore-worker/src/mpc_ckd.rs` `ensure_customer_loaded` →
   `assert_serving_allowed` reads `is_vault_verified` and
   `vault.get_state()` on every call, refuses on `unlocked == true`
   and evicts the cached master.
4. **No derivation after unlock** — `request_master` requires
   `!self.unlocked` and a self-call; the swap removed every TEE key.
5. **MPC CKD is deterministic** — the same `(predecessor, derivation_path)`
   yields the same secret, so `customer-recovery` reaches the master
   the keystore used.

The coordinator's `/call` pre-check
(`outlayer-coordinator/src/handlers/call.rs`,
`assert_secret_vault_serving_allowed`, private repo) is a fast-fail in
front of property 3, not a security boundary.

The whole procedure runs end-to-end on testnet in
[`tests/unified_vault_e2e.sh`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/tests/unified_vault_e2e.sh): V3
(finalize → keystore refuses → MPC recovery → offline re-derivation of
the wallet addresses), V5 (the same for a `wk_` wallet, ending with a
real transfer signed by the recovered key), V4 (secret decryption
after recovery).

---

## Files referenced from this document

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [`scripts/customer-recovery/`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/tree/main/scripts/customer-recovery/) | Standalone MPC CKD + key derivation + secret decrypt tool |
| [`scripts/customer-recovery/walkthrough.sh`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/scripts/customer-recovery/walkthrough.sh) | Interactive runbook for Phase A + B.1 |
| [`scripts/customer-recovery/README.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/scripts/customer-recovery/README.md) | CLI reference for the tool |

| [`VAULTS.md`](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/VAULTS.md) | Architecture and trust model |

<!-- source: VRF.md -->
> Source: https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/VRF.md

# OutLayer VRF — Verifiable Random Function

Cryptographically provable randomness for NEAR smart contracts.
Anyone can verify the proof on-chain: the output was produced by OutLayer's VRF key for exactly this alpha, and cannot have been re-rolled. That the output was unpredictable rests on the VRF key staying inside attested enclaves — see [Unpredictable without the key](#2-unpredictable-without-the-key).

## How it works

```
WASI Module                    Worker (TEE)                  Keystore (TEE)
    |                              |                              |
    |  vrf::random("coin-flip")    |                              |
    |----------------------------->|                              |
    |                              |  alpha = "vrf:42:alice.near:coin-flip"
    |                              |  POST /vrf/generate {alpha}  |
    |                              |----------------------------->|
    |                              |                              |  signature = Ed25519_sign(vrf_sk, alpha)
    |                              |                              |  output    = SHA256(signature)
    |                              |  {output_hex, signature_hex} |
    |                              |<-----------------------------|
    |  VrfOutput {                 |
    |    output_hex,               |
    |    signature_hex,            |
    |    alpha                     |
    |  }                           |
    |<-----------------------------|

On-chain verification:
    env::ed25519_verify(signature, alpha.as_bytes(), vrf_pubkey)  // native NEAR host function
```

### Alpha format

```
vrf:{request_id}:{sender_id}:{user_seed}
```

- **request_id** — the contract's request id (on-chain request) or the numeric request id the coordinator assigns to an HTTPS call. Auto-injected by worker, WASM cannot set it.
- **sender_id** — the paying account: the transaction's sender (blockchain) or the payment key owner (HTTPS). It is not the bound name a `use_bound_identity` run uses. Auto-injected by worker.
- **user_seed** — arbitrary string from developer's WASM module. Must not contain `:`.

Example: `vrf:98321:alice.near:coin-flip`

### Cryptographic primitives

| Primitive | Usage |
|-----------|-------|
| HMAC-SHA256 | Key derivation: `HMAC-SHA256(master_secret, "vrf-key")` → 32 bytes → Ed25519 keypair |
| Ed25519 (RFC 8032) | Deterministic signature: `sign(vrf_sk, alpha)` → 64-byte signature |
| SHA-256 | Output derivation: `SHA256(signature)` → 32-byte random output |

## Security properties

### 1. Deterministic — no re-rolling

Ed25519 signatures are deterministic per RFC 8032. Same key + same alpha = same signature = same output. The worker cannot retry to get a different result.

### 2. Unpredictable without the key

The VRF private key is derived inside the keystore TEE (Intel TDX) from the keystore's shared master secret via `HMAC-SHA256(master_secret, "vrf-key")` — always the default OutLayer master, never a customer vault's. The master secret is issued by the NEAR MPC network (chain-key derivation), where no single node holds it.

Stage caveat: `dao.outlayer.near` currently also carries a full-access key that can obtain the shared master outside an enclave, and measurement approval is owner-only (see [docs/NON_CUSTODIAL.md](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/docs/NON_CUSTODIAL.md#governance-at-this-stage)). Whoever holds the master can compute the VRF output for any alpha in advance. Verification proves the output was not re-rolled; it does not prove nobody could predict it.

### 3. Non-manipulable alpha

The WASM module only provides `user_seed`. The worker auto-prepends `request_id` and `sender_id`. The WASM guest cannot change these values. On an on-chain request `request_id` comes from the contract's event; on an HTTPS call it is assigned by the coordinator.

This means:
- Same seed by different users → different output (sender_id differs)
- Same seed in different requests → different output (request_id differs)
- A WASM module cannot forge an alpha to replay a previous result

### 4. Publicly verifiable

Anyone can verify the VRF output — no trust in the TEE required:

```
ed25519_verify(vrf_pubkey, alpha, signature) == true
SHA256(signature) == output
```

The VRF public key is available at `GET /vrf/pubkey` and can be hardcoded in smart contracts.

### 5. Consistent across keystore instances

All keystore instances derive the VRF keypair from the same master secret with the fixed seed `"vrf-key"`. This means:
- All instances produce the same VRF public key
- Any instance can generate the same output for the same alpha
- Keystore restarts don't change the key (the key changes only if the master secret does)

### 6. Rate-limited

Max 10 VRF calls per WASM execution. Prevents abuse of the signing endpoint.

## Developer guide

### SDK usage (Rust WASI module)

Add `outlayer` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
outlayer = "0.2"
```

Generate random output:

```rust
use outlayer::vrf;

// Get verifiable random output
let result = vrf::random("my-seed")?;
println!("Random: {}", result.output_hex);       // SHA256(signature), 32 bytes hex
println!("Proof:  {}", result.signature_hex);     // Ed25519 signature, 64 bytes hex
println!("Alpha:  {}", result.alpha);             // "vrf:{request_id}:{sender_id}:my-seed"

// Or get raw bytes
let (bytes, signature_hex, alpha) = vrf::random_bytes("my-seed")?;
// bytes: [u8; 32] — use for random number generation

// Get VRF public key (for including in output)
let pubkey = vrf::public_key()?;
```

Map to a range (e.g. 0..=99):

```rust
let result = vrf::random("roll")?;
let first_4_bytes = u32::from_be_bytes(hex_to_bytes(&result.output_hex[..8]));
let roll = (first_4_bytes as u64 * 100 / (u32::MAX as u64 + 1)) as u32; // 0..=99
```

Multiple independent random values — use unique sub-seeds:

```rust
for i in 0..5 {
    let result = vrf::random(&format!("card:{}", i))?;
    // Each call gets a unique alpha → unique output
}
```

### Constraints

- `user_seed` must not contain `:` (used as alpha delimiter)
- Max 10 VRF calls per execution
- VRF requires the keystore — the module must run on OutLayer workers (a component that imports `near:vrf/api` fails to start where VRF is unavailable)

### On-chain verification (NEAR smart contract)

```rust
use near_sdk::env;

fn verify_vrf(
    vrf_pubkey: &[u8; 32],   // from GET /vrf/pubkey or hardcoded
    alpha: &str,              // from VRF output
    signature: &[u8; 64],    // from VRF output (signature_hex decoded)
) -> bool {
    // NEAR native ed25519_verify
    env::ed25519_verify(signature, alpha.as_bytes(), vrf_pubkey)
}
```

Full contract example — see [wasi-examples/vrf-example/vrf-contract/](https://github.com/out-layer/vrf-example/tree/main/vrf-contract/).

### Deploying a contract with VRF

**Step 1.** Get the VRF public key:

```bash
# Mainnet
curl -s https://api.outlayer.ai/vrf/pubkey | jq -r .vrf_public_key_hex

# Testnet
curl -s https://testnet-api.outlayer.ai/vrf/pubkey | jq -r .vrf_public_key_hex
```

**Step 2.** Initialize contract with the pubkey:

```bash
near call my-vrf.near new '{
  "outlayer_contract_id": "outlayer.near",
  "project_id": "alice.near/vrf-ark",
  "vrf_pubkey_hex": "a1b2c3d4..."
}' --accountId my-vrf.near
```

**Step 3.** Verify it was stored:

```bash
near view my-vrf.near get_vrf_pubkey
# "a1b2c3d4..."
```

If the keystore rotates the VRF key (rare), update via `set_vrf_pubkey` (contract owner only):

```bash
near call my-vrf.near set_vrf_pubkey '{"vrf_pubkey_hex": "new_key_hex..."}' --accountId my-vrf.near
```

### Complete example: coin flip with on-chain verification

**WASI module** — generates VRF random number:
```rust
use outlayer::vrf;

let result = vrf::random("coin-flip")?;
// Map to 0 (Heads) or 1 (Tails)
let bytes = u32::from_be_bytes(/* first 4 bytes of output_hex */);
let side = (bytes as u64 * 2 / (u32::MAX as u64 + 1)) as u32;
```

**NEAR contract** — requests execution and verifies:
```rust
// 1. Request execution
ext_outlayer::ext(outlayer_contract_id)
    .with_attached_deposit(NearToken::from_millinear(10))
    .request_execution(
        json!({"Project": {"project_id": "alice.near/vrf-ark"}}),
        Some(resource_limits),
        Some(r#"{"seed":"coin-flip","max":1}"#.to_string()),
        None,
        Some("Json".to_string()),
        Some(player.clone()),
    )
    .then(ext_self::ext(current_account_id()).on_vrf_result(player, choice));

// 2. In callback — verify proof
let entry = &vrf_response.results[0];
let sig_bytes: [u8; 64] = hex::decode(&entry.signature_hex).try_into().unwrap();
let valid = env::ed25519_verify(&sig_bytes, entry.alpha.as_bytes(), &self.vrf_pubkey);
assert!(valid, "VRF proof verification failed");
```

## User verification guide

### 1. Get the VRF public key

```bash
curl https://api.outlayer.ai/vrf/pubkey
# {"vrf_public_key_hex":"a1b2c3d4..."}  (64 hex chars = 32 bytes)
```

### 2. Verify Ed25519 signature

Given a VRF result:
```json
{
  "value": 0,
  "signature_hex": "abcd...1234",
  "alpha": "vrf:98321:alice.near:coin-flip"
}
```

**Python (PyNaCl):**
```python
from nacl.signing import VerifyKey
import hashlib

vrf_pubkey_hex = "..."   # from /vrf/pubkey
signature_hex = "..."     # from result
alpha = "vrf:98321:alice.near:coin-flip"

vrf_pubkey = bytes.fromhex(vrf_pubkey_hex)
signature = bytes.fromhex(signature_hex)

# Verify: Ed25519 signature over alpha
verify_key = VerifyKey(vrf_pubkey)
verify_key.verify(alpha.encode(), signature)  # raises if invalid
print("Signature VALID")

# Verify: output = SHA256(signature)
output = hashlib.sha256(signature).hexdigest()
print(f"Output: {output}")

# If mapped to range: first 4 bytes → u32 → scale
first_4 = int(output[:8], 16)
mapped = first_4 * (max_value + 1) // (2**32)
print(f"Mapped value: {mapped}")
```

**JavaScript (tweetnacl):**
```javascript
import nacl from 'tweetnacl';
import { createHash } from 'crypto';

const vrfPubkey = Buffer.from(vrfPubkeyHex, 'hex');
const signature = Buffer.from(signatureHex, 'hex');
const alpha = Buffer.from('vrf:98321:alice.near:coin-flip');

// Verify signature
const valid = nacl.sign.detached.verify(alpha, signature, vrfPubkey);
console.log('Valid:', valid);

// Verify output
const output = createHash('sha256').update(signature).digest('hex');
console.log('Output:', output);
```

**NEAR contract (on-chain):**
```rust
let valid = env::ed25519_verify(&signature_bytes, alpha.as_bytes(), &vrf_pubkey_bytes);
```

### 3. Verify alpha integrity

The alpha `vrf:{request_id}:{sender_id}:{user_seed}` contains:
- **request_id** — visible in the `execution_requested` event of the `request_execution` call (on-chain requests; for an HTTPS call it is the coordinator's id and cannot be checked against the chain)
- **sender_id** — the account that paid for the request
- **user_seed** — the seed from the WASM input

Reconstruct and compare:
```python
expected_alpha = f"vrf:{request_id}:{sender_id}:{user_seed}"
assert alpha == expected_alpha, "Alpha mismatch — possible tampering"
```

### Verification checklist

1. `ed25519_verify(vrf_pubkey, alpha, signature)` — signature is valid
2. `SHA256(signature) == output_hex` — output matches signature
3. Alpha contains correct `request_id` from the blockchain event (on-chain requests)
4. Alpha contains correct `sender_id` (the caller)
5. VRF public key matches `GET /vrf/pubkey`

If all 5 checks pass, the output is the one OutLayer's VRF key gives for this alpha: it was not re-rolled or swapped after the fact. Unpredictability depends on the key's custody (see above).

## API reference

| Endpoint | Method | Auth | Response |
|----------|--------|------|----------|
| `/vrf/pubkey` | GET | Public | `{"vrf_public_key_hex": "..."}` |

SDK functions:

| Function | Returns | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `vrf::random(seed)` | `Result<VrfOutput>` | Random output + proof |
| `vrf::random_bytes(seed)` | `Result<([u8; 32], String, String)>` | Raw bytes + signature + alpha |
| `vrf::public_key()` | `Result<String>` | VRF public key hex |

- Crypto: [keystore-worker/src/crypto.rs](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/keystore-worker/src/crypto.rs) — `vrf_generate`, `vrf_public_key_hex`
- Host functions: [worker/src/outlayer_vrf/host_functions.rs](https://github.com/out-layer/outlayer/blob/main/worker/src/outlayer_vrf/host_functions.rs)

- Example WASI: [wasi-examples/vrf-example/](https://github.com/out-layer/vrf-example/)
